# Forensic dossier — Fugro N.V. (FUR.AS, Euronext Amsterdam)

**Prepared:** 27 July 2026 · **Live price used:** EUR 9.50 (Euronext Amsterdam, euros; previous close EUR 9.71) · **Market value:** about EUR 1.06 billion on roughly 111.3 million shares · **52-week range:** EUR 8.10–12.87

**A note on sources before anything else.** Fugro is a Dutch company that reports twice a year, and no earnings-call transcript for this listing exists in our licensed data feed — the transcript service returns nothing for the ticker, and there is no news coverage of it either. This dossier is therefore built on dated primary documents rather than call transcripts: the full-year 2025 results release of 27 February 2026, the first-quarter 2026 trading update of 23 April 2026, the company's published outlook page, its investor calendar, and the audited financial statements. Every quotation below is taken from those written releases, and each one is dated. Where the usual transcript evidence would be required — tone shifts inside a call, questions management dodged — I say plainly that the evidence does not exist rather than invent it.

**What the company does.** Fugro is the world's largest provider of what the industry calls site characterisation: it maps and tests the seabed and the ground before anyone builds on it. Before a wind farm, an oil platform, a subsea cable, a bridge or a port is built, someone has to survey the seabed, drill and test the soil, and certify that the structure will stand. Fugro does that with a fleet of specialist survey vessels, drilling rigs, remotely operated underwater vehicles and laboratories, employing about 9,060 people worldwide. It is a services business that bids project by project — not a licensor, not a subscription business.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

The story Fugro told the market between 2021 and 2024 was an energy-transition growth story, and for three years the numbers backed it. Revenue went from EUR 1.46 billion in 2021 to EUR 2.28 billion in 2024, a 56% increase in three years. Operating profit — earnings before interest and tax, the profit the business makes from trading before financing costs — went from EUR 80 million to EUR 315 million over the same span, and the operating margin more than tripled, from 5.5% to 13.8%. The engine was offshore wind: governments across Europe, Asia and the United States were awarding seabed leases, and every lease needed Fugro's early-stage survey work before a turbine could be sited.

That story broke in 2025, and it broke on the demand side rather than the competitive side. In the full-year release of 27 February 2026, chief executive Mark Heine described the year in one sentence: offshore wind "slowed significantly across several countries, reducing demand for early-stage site characterisation work." Revenue fell to EUR 1,848.1 million, down EUR 427.3 million or 16.1% on a comparable basis. Operating profit fell to EUR 90.9 million and the margin to 4.9%. After EUR 113.6 million of one-off charges, mostly impairments, the company reported a net loss of EUR 20.4 million, or minus 18 euro cents a share — its first loss since 2020.

Three things have quietly changed in what management emphasises, and they matter more than the headline decline:

- **The growth driver has been swapped.** Offshore wind is no longer presented as the engine; gas is. In the same February 2026 release the chief executive wrote that "the complexity of the energy transition and rising global demand suggest that fossil fuels, especially gas, will remain significant for the foreseeable future." A company that spent three years selling itself as an energy-transition beneficiary now leans on hydrocarbon durability. That is an honest adjustment to reality, but it is a thesis reversal, and investors who bought the transition story own something different now.
- **The story has shifted from growth to self-help.** The February 2026 and April 2026 releases lead with cost, capital spending and cash, not with orders and expansion. The company completed a cost-reduction programme delivering EUR 120 million of annual savings and cutting 1,050 full-time positions, and it guided 2026 capital spending down to EUR 150–165 million from EUR 248 million in 2025.
- **The recovery language is deliberately hedged.** In the 23 April 2026 first-quarter update, the chief executive said the offshore wind market "is showing early signs of recovery" but that "the near term is likely to focus on industry realignment" — and the outlook page adds that "it will take some time for increased site characterisation work to materialise." That is management telling you, in plain words, not to expect the order book to turn this year.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials — the forensic test

Holding a cash margin up while revenue falls is real evidence the cost work landed. | Supported |
| Margin improvement is expected in 2026 from those cost measures (2026 outlook, 23 Apr 2026) | The operating margin went the *other* way in the first quarter: minus 0.4%, against plus 0.2% a year earlier. First-quarter free cash flow — cash from operations after capital spending — was minus EUR 57.9 million, better than the minus EUR 84.4 million of a year earlier, which is directionally consistent. | Credible but unproven; the 31 July print is the first real test |

**The claim that fails hardest is one management never made out loud — the capital-allocation claim implied by its actions.** In 2025 Fugro spent EUR 247.7 million on capital projects into a revenue line that was collapsing, generated EUR 104.6 million of operating cash, and therefore burned EUR 136.6 million of free cash. It then paid EUR 83.6 million of dividends and bought back EUR 13.3 million of its own stock out of that hole, and funded the gap by drawing EUR 307.5 million of new long-term debt. Net debt roughly quadrupled. Paying a dividend with borrowed money while the order book shrinks is the clearest capital-allocation error in this file, and it is why the balance sheet is now the binding constraint rather than a source of optionality. The dividend was subsequently cut roughly 80%, to 15 euro cents from 75 cents, approved at the annual meeting on 23 April 2026 — the right decision, taken a year late.

And the screener's net debt of EUR 413 million overstates the audited figure of EUR 382.5 million. Neither number should be used.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: declining, and declining honestly rather than evasively.**

I do not have call transcripts, so I cannot grade tone inside a question-and-answer session. What I can grade is the written commentary, and the direction there is unambiguous. In the 27 February 2026 full-year release the language is retrospective and damage-describing: offshore wind "slowed significantly across several countries." By the 23 April 2026 first-quarter update the language is defensive and heavily qualified: the market "is showing early signs of recovery," but "the near term is likely to focus on industry realignment," and separately, "it will take some time for increased site characterisation work to materialise."

That is three hedges stacked on one recovery claim. Read plainly, management is signalling that the improvement in 2026 must come from its own cost base rather than from customer demand — which is exactly what the guidance says: margin improvement "driven by the impact of implemented cost measures and operational efficiencies," with no revenue-growth claim attached.

The shift from offensive to defensive vocabulary is complete. Nothing in the 2026 communications talks about capacity expansion, fleet investment or market share. Everything talks about cost, capital discipline, working capital and cash.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: medium.** The record splits cleanly into two halves.

*What management promised and delivered:* the cost programme. A EUR 120 million annualised saving with 1,050 positions removed was announced and then confirmed complete, and the first-quarter cash margin improvement corroborates it. That is a hard, checkable promise kept.

*What management got wrong:* the cycle, and the capital plan built on it. Capital spending ran at EUR 248 million in 2025 — above the EUR 182 million of 2023 and only slightly below the EUR 264 million of the 2024 peak — while revenue fell 16%. ## 5. Analyst pressure points

Without transcripts I cannot report what analysts pushed on in a call. What the published record does show is where the disclosure is thinnest, and that is a fair proxy for where the pressure sits:

- **No quantified market or regional split in the 2025 release.** The company describes offshore wind's decline qualitatively but the release does not break revenue down by end market. An investor cannot independently size how much of the business is offshore wind, how much is oil and gas, and how much is infrastructure and water. For a company whose entire investment case turns on the mix between a collapsed market and a durable one, that is a material gap.
- **No net debt figure in the first-quarter update.** Free cash flow of minus EUR 57.9 million is disclosed; the resulting leverage is not. Adding that burn and the roughly EUR 17 million dividend to the EUR 382 million year-end position implies net debt somewhere around EUR 450 million by mid-year, or roughly 1.7 times cash profit — above the company's own 1.5 times ceiling. Leaving that arithmetic to the reader, in the quarter it first goes the wrong way, is a disclosure choice worth noticing.
- **No path published from a minus 0.4% operating margin to the 8%-plus the market expects for the year.** The consensus of six analysts has 2026 operating profit at about EUR 149 million on revenue of about EUR 1.80 billion — a 64% increase in profit on a slightly *lower* revenue line, after a first quarter that lost money at the operating line. Management has not shown the bridge.
- **A governance blemish, small but noted:** on 30 April 2026 the company disclosed a voting-registration error affecting a resolution at the annual meeting held a week earlier. It appears procedural rather than substantive, but it is the kind of administrative slip that erodes patience in a year when nothing else is going right.

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- Free cash flow has been negative for five consecutive reported periods: minus EUR 136.6 million across 2025 and minus EUR 57.9 million in the first quarter of 2026.
- Net debt went from EUR 96 million to EUR 382 million during 2025, and cash fell from EUR 319.5 million to EUR 93.2 million. Leverage of 1.4 times sits at the company's self-imposed ceiling of 1.5 times before the seasonally cash-hungry first half is added.
- The operating margin in the first quarter of 2026 was *worse* than a year earlier, at minus 0.4% against plus 0.2%, despite the full EUR 120 million of savings being in place. Depreciation from boom-era capital spending is consuming the self-help.
- The order book is still shrinking: minus 5.7% comparable at year-end 2025 and a further minus 3.5% in the first quarter of 2026.
- Return on invested capital — profit relative to the money tied up in the business — is 1.2% on a trailing basis. Even at the mid-cycle profit the market expects for 2027, it recovers only to roughly 8% after tax, which is about the company's cost of capital. This is the finding that most constrains the value case, and section 8 returns to it.
- EUR 182.7 million of deferred tax assets sit on the balance sheet — future tax relief that is only worth anything if profits return. If 2026 disappoints, part of that is impairable, and it would come straight out of the book value that underpins the cheapness argument.
- A dividend was paid out of borrowed money in 2025, then cut roughly 80%.

**Green flags**

- The cost programme was real, delivered, and is visible in the cash margin: 10.4% in the first quarter of 2026 against 9.8% a year earlier, on lower revenue.
- Capital spending guidance of EUR 150–165 million for 2026 is a EUR 83–98 million reduction against 2025. Against a EUR 1.06 billion market value, that swing alone is worth roughly 8–9% of the company in annual free cash flow, and it requires no revenue recovery whatsoever. It is the most mechanical, least narrative-dependent part of the case.
- The first-quarter cash burn improved year on year, from minus EUR 84.4 million to minus EUR 57.9 million.
- The dividend reset, however late, removes the obligation that was consuming the balance sheet.
- The end markets are cyclical and policy-driven, not structurally dying. Gas-related demand is durable on the company's own account, European offshore wind tendering is reportedly picking up, and infrastructure and water work is steady. Nothing here is being replaced by a cheaper technology.

## 7. Hidden signals

- **The gap between the cash line and the profit line is the whole story.** Cash profit of EUR 267.9 million in 2025 against operating profit of EUR 90.9 million means depreciation and amortisation of EUR 177 million — about two-thirds of cash profit. Fugro is far more capital-intensive than its own cash-margin headline implies, and every euro of the boom-era fleet investment now shows up as a charge against profit for years. When management leads with the cash margin and the market quotes the cash margin, both are describing a number that flatters this business by roughly seven percentage points.
- **The vocabulary has moved from "market" to "industry realignment."** Realignment is what an industry does when capacity has to leave, not what a market does when demand returns. Management chose that word in April 2026 rather than a growth word, and I read it as an honest signal that customer consolidation, not customer spending, is the near-term event.
- **Cash was substituted for balance-sheet flexibility, not for growth.** Long-term borrowings of EUR 307.5 million were drawn in 2025 while EUR 215.6 million of short-term debt was repaid and EUR 96.9 million went out as dividends and buybacks. That is a refinancing exercise dressed as a normal year, and it is why the 2026 capital-spending cut is not optional.
- **A shrinking business is now paying for a fleet sized for a bigger one.** Property, plant and equipment stands at EUR 1,086 million net — larger than in 2023 — against revenue that has fallen 19% from the peak. Either revenue comes back to that fleet, or the fleet has to come down to the revenue. There is no third path, and the second one means further impairments.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict — for the director

**Trajectory: deteriorating, with a credible but so-far unproven turn underway.**

Every headline measure is still moving the wrong way — revenue, order book, operating margin, free cash flow, net debt, dividend. The management response is genuine and well-chosen: cost out, capital spending halved, dividend reset, and the strategic emphasis rotated from offshore wind toward gas and infrastructure. But a first-quarter operating margin that went *backwards* despite EUR 120 million of completed savings is not yet a turn. It becomes one on the day the depreciation drag stops outrunning the cost savings, and that day has a date: 31 July 2026.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing this position is not the cycle — it is the return on capital.** Over the five years 2021 through 2025, Fugro's average operating profit was about EUR 169 million against invested capital of roughly EUR 1.46 billion. After tax that is a return of roughly 8.7% — right on top of a reasonable cost of capital for a Dutch cyclical services business carrying 1.4 times leverage. The consensus mid-cycle year, 2027, implies almost exactly the same thing: EUR 157 million of operating profit, about 8.1% after tax on invested capital. That single fact reframes the whole investment. A business that earns its cost of capital through the cycle is worth roughly the capital invested in it — that is, roughly its book value — and no more. Book value is EUR 11.83 a share and the stock is EUR 9.50, so the honest discount here is about 20%, not the 100%-plus that a 0.78 times revenue multiple or a 6.6 times cash-profit multiple superficially suggests. Anyone underwriting this as a doubling is implicitly assuming Fugro returns to 2024's 13.8% margin and stays there; the five-year record says 2024 was the peak, not the norm.

**Economic moat: narrow, and currently eroding.** The moat type is scale-cost combined with an intangible data and certification asset. Fugro owns the largest specialist survey fleet in the world, holds more than sixty years of accumulated geotechnical records on seabeds and soils that competitors cannot replicate, and carries the safety accreditations and client qualifications that gate entry to major offshore programmes. Those are real barriers — this is not a commodity contractor. But the moat is narrow, and the evidence says it is currently eroding rather than stable: gross margin is contracting, return on invested capital has fallen from roughly 16% after tax at the 2024 peak to 1.2% on a trailing basis, and the operating margin turned negative in the first quarter of 2026 even with the cost base already reduced. A genuinely wide moat holds price when volume falls. Fugro's did not.

**Secular threat: manageable — this is a fear-print, not a melting base.** The distinction matters. Offshore wind did not disappear because a better technology replaced seabed surveying; it slowed because project economics broke at higher interest rates and because policy support was withdrawn in some markets, most obviously the United States, which the company describes as dormant under the current administration. Gas-related demand is, on the company's own reading, durable for the foreseeable future, and infrastructure and water work is steady. The one structural question worth monitoring is whether uncrewed survey vessels, satellite-derived data and automated interpretation eventually deflate the price of the service itself — Fugro is deploying those tools rather than being disrupted by them, but they are cost-deflationary for the whole industry over a decade. That is a medium-term margin question, not a terminal-value question. The cheapness here is a fear-print on a cyclically broken franchise, not a low multiple on a structurally shrinking base — which is to say, not a value trap. It is simply a business whose fair value is close to its book value, trading at a modest discount to it.

# Forensic dossier — Fugro N.V. (FUR.AS, Euronext Amsterdam)

**Prepared:** 27 July 2026 · **Live price used:** EUR 9.50 (Euronext Amsterdam, euros; previous close EUR 9.71) · **Market value:** about EUR 1.06 billion on roughly 111.3 million shares · **52-week range:** EUR 8.10–12.87

**A note on sources before anything else.** Fugro is a Dutch company that reports twice a year, and no earnings-call transcript for this listing exists in our licensed data feed — the transcript service returns nothing for the ticker, and there is no news coverage of it either. This dossier is therefore built on dated primary documents rather than call transcripts: the full-year 2025 results release of 27 February 2026, the first-quarter 2026 trading update of 23 April 2026, the company's published outlook page, its investor calendar, and the audited financial statements. Every quotation below is taken from those written releases, and each one is dated. Where the usual transcript evidence would be required — tone shifts inside a call, questions management dodged — I say plainly that the evidence does not exist rather than invent it.

**What the company does.** Fugro is the world's largest provider of what the industry calls site characterisation: it maps and tests the seabed and the ground before anyone builds on it. Before a wind farm, an oil platform, a subsea cable, a bridge or a port is built, someone has to survey the seabed, drill and test the soil, and certify that the structure will stand. Fugro does that with a fleet of specialist survey vessels, drilling rigs, remotely operated underwater vehicles and laboratories, employing about 9,060 people worldwide. It is a services business that bids project by project — not a licensor, not a subscription business.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

The story Fugro told the market between 2021 and 2024 was an energy-transition growth story, and for three years the numbers backed it. Revenue went from EUR 1.46 billion in 2021 to EUR 2.28 billion in 2024, a 56% increase in three years. Operating profit — earnings before interest and tax, the profit the business makes from trading before financing costs — went from EUR 80 million to EUR 315 million over the same span, and the operating margin more than tripled, from 5.5% to 13.8%. The engine was offshore wind: governments across Europe, Asia and the United States were awarding seabed leases, and every lease needed Fugro's early-stage survey work before a turbine could be sited.

That story broke in 2025, and it broke on the demand side rather than the competitive side. In the full-year release of 27 February 2026, chief executive Mark Heine described the year in one sentence: offshore wind "slowed significantly across several countries, reducing demand for early-stage site characterisation work." Revenue fell to EUR 1,848.1 million, down EUR 427.3 million or 16.1% on a comparable basis. Operating profit fell to EUR 90.9 million and the margin to 4.9%. After EUR 113.6 million of one-off charges, mostly impairments, the company reported a net loss of EUR 20.4 million, or minus 18 euro cents a share — its first loss since 2020.

Three things have quietly changed in what management emphasises, and they matter more than the headline decline:

- **The growth driver has been swapped.** Offshore wind is no longer presented as the engine; gas is. In the same February 2026 release the chief executive wrote that "the complexity of the energy transition and rising global demand suggest that fossil fuels, especially gas, will remain significant for the foreseeable future." A company that spent three years selling itself as an energy-transition beneficiary now leans on hydrocarbon durability. That is an honest adjustment to reality, but it is a thesis reversal, and investors who bought the transition story own something different now.
- **The story has shifted from growth to self-help.** The February 2026 and April 2026 releases lead with cost, capital spending and cash, not with orders and expansion. The company completed a cost-reduction programme delivering EUR 120 million of annual savings and cutting 1,050 full-time positions, and it guided 2026 capital spending down to EUR 150–165 million from EUR 248 million in 2025.
- **The recovery language is deliberately hedged.** In the 23 April 2026 first-quarter update, the chief executive said the offshore wind market "is showing early signs of recovery" but that "the near term is likely to focus on industry realignment" — and the outlook page adds that "it will take some time for increased site characterisation work to materialise." That is management telling you, in plain words, not to expect the order book to turn this year.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials — the forensic test

| Management claim (with date) | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| A EUR 120 million cost-reduction programme has been completed, with 1,050 positions removed (27 Feb 2026, restated 23 Apr 2026) | The savings are visible where you would expect them first: the cash-profit margin — earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, which strips out the accounting charge for wearing out the fleet — rose to 10.4% in the first quarter of 2026 from 9.8% a year earlier, on 2.1% lower comparable revenue. Holding a cash margin up while revenue falls is real evidence the cost work landed. | Supported |
| Margin improvement is expected in 2026 from those cost measures (2026 outlook, 23 Apr 2026) | The operating margin went the *other* way in the first quarter: minus 0.4%, against plus 0.2% a year earlier. The cash-margin gain was more than eaten by depreciation on the fleet Fugro built during the boom. | Not yet supported — the gap between the cash line and the profit line is the single most important number in this file |
| Capital spending falls to EUR 150–165 million in 2026 from EUR 248 million (27 Feb 2026 and 23 Apr 2026) | Untested. Nothing in the first-quarter update confirms or contradicts it. First-quarter free cash flow — cash from operations after capital spending — was minus EUR 57.9 million, better than the minus EUR 84.4 million of a year earlier, which is directionally consistent. | Credible but unproven; the 31 July print is the first real test |
| The balance sheet is robust, with a policy of keeping net debt below 1.5 times cash profit (published outlook) | Net debt was EUR 382 million at 31 December 2025, giving 1.4 times — inside the ceiling, but only just, and up from roughly EUR 96 million a year earlier. Cash fell from EUR 319.5 million to EUR 93.2 million in a single year. | Technically true, materially strained |
| Offshore wind is showing early signs of recovery (23 Apr 2026) | The order book says otherwise so far. The twelve-month backlog was EUR 1,395.9 million at year-end 2025, down 5.7% comparable, and EUR 1,385.1 million at the end of the first quarter of 2026, down a further 3.5% comparable. Recovery has not reached the contracted work. | Forward-looking and unfalsifiable today; the backlog is the honest scoreboard and it is still shrinking |

**The claim that fails hardest is one management never made out loud — the capital-allocation claim implied by its actions.** In 2025 Fugro spent EUR 247.7 million on capital projects into a revenue line that was collapsing, generated EUR 104.6 million of operating cash, and therefore burned EUR 136.6 million of free cash. It then paid EUR 83.6 million of dividends and bought back EUR 13.3 million of its own stock out of that hole, and funded the gap by drawing EUR 307.5 million of new long-term debt. Net debt roughly quadrupled. Paying a dividend with borrowed money while the order book shrinks is the clearest capital-allocation error in this file, and it is why the balance sheet is now the binding constraint rather than a source of optionality. The dividend was subsequently cut roughly 80%, to 15 euro cents from 75 cents, approved at the annual meeting on 23 April 2026 — the right decision, taken a year late.

**Two data corrections for anyone reading the screener output.** The screener line reporting trailing twelve-month diluted earnings of EUR 2.21 a share is stale and wrong: the audited 2025 figure is minus 18 euro cents. And the screener's net debt of EUR 413 million overstates the audited figure of EUR 382.5 million. Neither number should be used.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: declining, and declining honestly rather than evasively.**

I do not have call transcripts, so I cannot grade tone inside a question-and-answer session. What I can grade is the written commentary, and the direction there is unambiguous. In the 27 February 2026 full-year release the language is retrospective and damage-describing: offshore wind "slowed significantly across several countries." By the 23 April 2026 first-quarter update the language is defensive and heavily qualified: the market "is showing early signs of recovery," but "the near term is likely to focus on industry realignment," and separately, "it will take some time for increased site characterisation work to materialise."

That is three hedges stacked on one recovery claim. Read plainly, management is signalling that the improvement in 2026 must come from its own cost base rather than from customer demand — which is exactly what the guidance says: margin improvement "driven by the impact of implemented cost measures and operational efficiencies," with no revenue-growth claim attached.

The shift from offensive to defensive vocabulary is complete. Nothing in the 2026 communications talks about capacity expansion, fleet investment or market share. Everything talks about cost, capital discipline, working capital and cash.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: medium.** The record splits cleanly into two halves.

*What management promised and delivered:* the cost programme. A EUR 120 million annualised saving with 1,050 positions removed was announced and then confirmed complete, and the first-quarter cash margin improvement corroborates it. That is a hard, checkable promise kept.

*What management got wrong:* the cycle, and the capital plan built on it. Capital spending ran at EUR 248 million in 2025 — above the EUR 182 million of 2023 and only slightly below the EUR 264 million of the 2024 peak — while revenue fell 16%. Fleet capacity was added into a demand air pocket, and the depreciation charge from that decision is now the thing preventing the cost savings from reaching the operating profit line. The screener's note that the company beat expectations in three of its last four reporting periods reflects a low bar reset downward, not a sandbagging pattern; the absolute trajectory over the same window was down.

The company withdrew any specific revenue guidance for 2026 and now guides only qualitatively on margin, with hard numbers attached solely to capital spending. That is a rational response to poor visibility, but it also means there is very little to hold them to. The only falsifiable 2026 commitment is the EUR 150–165 million capital-spending range.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Without transcripts I cannot report what analysts pushed on in a call. What the published record does show is where the disclosure is thinnest, and that is a fair proxy for where the pressure sits:

- **No quantified market or regional split in the 2025 release.** The company describes offshore wind's decline qualitatively but the release does not break revenue down by end market. An investor cannot independently size how much of the business is offshore wind, how much is oil and gas, and how much is infrastructure and water. For a company whose entire investment case turns on the mix between a collapsed market and a durable one, that is a material gap.
- **No net debt figure in the first-quarter update.** Free cash flow of minus EUR 57.9 million is disclosed; the resulting leverage is not. Adding that burn and the roughly EUR 17 million dividend to the EUR 382 million year-end position implies net debt somewhere around EUR 450 million by mid-year, or roughly 1.7 times cash profit — above the company's own 1.5 times ceiling. Leaving that arithmetic to the reader, in the quarter it first goes the wrong way, is a disclosure choice worth noticing.
- **No path published from a minus 0.4% operating margin to the 8%-plus the market expects for the year.** The consensus of six analysts has 2026 operating profit at about EUR 149 million on revenue of about EUR 1.80 billion — a 64% increase in profit on a slightly *lower* revenue line, after a first quarter that lost money at the operating line. Management has not shown the bridge.
- **A governance blemish, small but noted:** on 30 April 2026 the company disclosed a voting-registration error affecting a resolution at the annual meeting held a week earlier. It appears procedural rather than substantive, but it is the kind of administrative slip that erodes patience in a year when nothing else is going right.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- Free cash flow has been negative for five consecutive reported periods: minus EUR 136.6 million across 2025 and minus EUR 57.9 million in the first quarter of 2026.
- Net debt went from EUR 96 million to EUR 382 million during 2025, and cash fell from EUR 319.5 million to EUR 93.2 million. Leverage of 1.4 times sits at the company's self-imposed ceiling of 1.5 times before the seasonally cash-hungry first half is added.
- The operating margin in the first quarter of 2026 was *worse* than a year earlier, at minus 0.4% against plus 0.2%, despite the full EUR 120 million of savings being in place. Depreciation from boom-era capital spending is consuming the self-help.
- The order book is still shrinking: minus 5.7% comparable at year-end 2025 and a further minus 3.5% in the first quarter of 2026.
- Return on invested capital — profit relative to the money tied up in the business — is 1.2% on a trailing basis. Even at the mid-cycle profit the market expects for 2027, it recovers only to roughly 8% after tax, which is about the company's cost of capital. This is the finding that most constrains the value case, and section 8 returns to it.
- EUR 182.7 million of deferred tax assets sit on the balance sheet — future tax relief that is only worth anything if profits return. If 2026 disappoints, part of that is impairable, and it would come straight out of the book value that underpins the cheapness argument.
- A dividend was paid out of borrowed money in 2025, then cut roughly 80%.

**Green flags**

- The cost programme was real, delivered, and is visible in the cash margin: 10.4% in the first quarter of 2026 against 9.8% a year earlier, on lower revenue.
- Capital spending guidance of EUR 150–165 million for 2026 is a EUR 83–98 million reduction against 2025. Against a EUR 1.06 billion market value, that swing alone is worth roughly 8–9% of the company in annual free cash flow, and it requires no revenue recovery whatsoever. It is the most mechanical, least narrative-dependent part of the case.
- The first-quarter cash burn improved year on year, from minus EUR 84.4 million to minus EUR 57.9 million.
- The dividend reset, however late, removes the obligation that was consuming the balance sheet.
- The end markets are cyclical and policy-driven, not structurally dying. Gas-related demand is durable on the company's own account, European offshore wind tendering is reportedly picking up, and infrastructure and water work is steady. Nothing here is being replaced by a cheaper technology.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

- **The gap between the cash line and the profit line is the whole story.** Cash profit of EUR 267.9 million in 2025 against operating profit of EUR 90.9 million means depreciation and amortisation of EUR 177 million — about two-thirds of cash profit. Fugro is far more capital-intensive than its own cash-margin headline implies, and every euro of the boom-era fleet investment now shows up as a charge against profit for years. When management leads with the cash margin and the market quotes the cash margin, both are describing a number that flatters this business by roughly seven percentage points.
- **The vocabulary has moved from "market" to "industry realignment."** Realignment is what an industry does when capacity has to leave, not what a market does when demand returns. Management chose that word in April 2026 rather than a growth word, and I read it as an honest signal that customer consolidation, not customer spending, is the near-term event.
- **Cash was substituted for balance-sheet flexibility, not for growth.** Long-term borrowings of EUR 307.5 million were drawn in 2025 while EUR 215.6 million of short-term debt was repaid and EUR 96.9 million went out as dividends and buybacks. That is a refinancing exercise dressed as a normal year, and it is why the 2026 capital-spending cut is not optional.
- **A shrinking business is now paying for a fleet sized for a bigger one.** Property, plant and equipment stands at EUR 1,086 million net — larger than in 2023 — against revenue that has fallen 19% from the peak. Either revenue comes back to that fleet, or the fleet has to come down to the revenue. There is no third path, and the second one means further impairments.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict — for the director

**Trajectory: deteriorating, with a credible but so-far unproven turn underway.**

Every headline measure is still moving the wrong way — revenue, order book, operating margin, free cash flow, net debt, dividend. The management response is genuine and well-chosen: cost out, capital spending halved, dividend reset, and the strategic emphasis rotated from offshore wind toward gas and infrastructure. But a first-quarter operating margin that went *backwards* despite EUR 120 million of completed savings is not yet a turn. It becomes one on the day the depreciation drag stops outrunning the cost savings, and that day has a date: 31 July 2026.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing this position is not the cycle — it is the return on capital.** Over the five years 2021 through 2025, Fugro's average operating profit was about EUR 169 million against invested capital of roughly EUR 1.46 billion. After tax that is a return of roughly 8.7% — right on top of a reasonable cost of capital for a Dutch cyclical services business carrying 1.4 times leverage. The consensus mid-cycle year, 2027, implies almost exactly the same thing: EUR 157 million of operating profit, about 8.1% after tax on invested capital. That single fact reframes the whole investment. A business that earns its cost of capital through the cycle is worth roughly the capital invested in it — that is, roughly its book value — and no more. Book value is EUR 11.83 a share and the stock is EUR 9.50, so the honest discount here is about 20%, not the 100%-plus that a 0.78 times revenue multiple or a 6.6 times cash-profit multiple superficially suggests. Anyone underwriting this as a doubling is implicitly assuming Fugro returns to 2024's 13.8% margin and stays there; the five-year record says 2024 was the peak, not the norm.

**Economic moat: narrow, and currently eroding.** The moat type is scale-cost combined with an intangible data and certification asset. Fugro owns the largest specialist survey fleet in the world, holds more than sixty years of accumulated geotechnical records on seabeds and soils that competitors cannot replicate, and carries the safety accreditations and client qualifications that gate entry to major offshore programmes. Those are real barriers — this is not a commodity contractor. But the moat is narrow, and the evidence says it is currently eroding rather than stable: gross margin is contracting, return on invested capital has fallen from roughly 16% after tax at the 2024 peak to 1.2% on a trailing basis, and the operating margin turned negative in the first quarter of 2026 even with the cost base already reduced. A genuinely wide moat holds price when volume falls. Fugro's did not.

**Secular threat: manageable — this is a fear-print, not a melting base.** The distinction matters. Offshore wind did not disappear because a better technology replaced seabed surveying; it slowed because project economics broke at higher interest rates and because policy support was withdrawn in some markets, most obviously the United States, which the company describes as dormant under the current administration. Gas-related demand is, on the company's own reading, durable for the foreseeable future, and infrastructure and water work is steady. The one structural question worth monitoring is whether uncrewed survey vessels, satellite-derived data and automated interpretation eventually deflate the price of the service itself — Fugro is deploying those tools rather than being disrupted by them, but they are cost-deflationary for the whole industry over a decade. That is a medium-term margin question, not a terminal-value question. The cheapness here is a fear-print on a cyclically broken franchise, not a low multiple on a structurally shrinking base — which is to say, not a value trap. It is simply a business whose fair value is close to its book value, trading at a modest discount to it.
